title: How To Allow For Open Class Discussion
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Responding to a common question about reconciling SCM's hand-raising rule with genuine open discussion, Linsin's central claim is that the two aren't actually in conflict — free-flowing conversation just needs to be deliberately carved out, named, and taught rather than allowed to happen spontaneously. His concrete three-step technique starts with defining a specific window called something like "open discussion time," complete with clear signals for when it opens and closes and an explicit note that the hand-raising rule is being set aside only within that narrow window. Second, he insists the actual skills of discussion — turn-taking, building on a peer's point, not interrupting — must be explicitly modeled by the teacher and a small demonstration group before the whole class attempts it. Third, he recommends starting practice with low-stakes, simple topics (his example: why mint chip ice cream is popular) before gradually scaling up to complex academic debates like the causes of the Civil War. The overall argument is that skipping any of these three steps is what turns open discussion into confusion or disaster, not the format itself.
points: Name and bound a specific "open discussion time" with clear open and close signals so it doesn't erode the hand-raising rule generally.
The mechanics of good discussion — turn-taking, not interrupting, building on others — must be explicitly taught and modeled first.
Practice should start with low-stakes, simple topics before scaling up to complex academic debate.
Confusion or chaos in open discussion is attributed to skipping these steps, not to the format of open discussion itself.
quotes: This is a great question because at first glance our classroom management plans don’t allow for open, back-and-forth interaction among students and teacher.
The answer is that it does leave room. You can indeed conduct free-flowing conversation in your classroom while still maintaining the integrity of the rule.
Give it a name, like “open discussion time.” Define precisely what it is and why it’s good for the class.
For open discussion to work, your students need to have the skills to navigate its jazz-like flow.
Try five minutes and choose simple, relatable topics like, for example, why mint chip ice cream is so popular.
